title: 3D Printable Golf Things
body:
A 3D printer turns a spool of plastic into golf gear. Two prints from the [open source golf landscape](/posts/open-source-golf-is-exploding/) are now part of my practice: a ball dispenser and a swing plane trainer. Both came off a Bambu Lab A1 mini.

## Golf Ball Dispenser Pro

[Golf Ball Dispenser Pro](https://makerworld.com/en/models/1295289-golf-ball-dispenser-pro) by christofer.jh is fully 3D printable. It needs no screws, springs or rubber bands, only golf balls. The magazine holds 25 balls and each press of the pedal places one on the tee. It is great for practicing into a net in the backyard or in a sim setup.

![The Golf Ball Dispenser Pro project open in the slicer for an A1 mini. Six plates hold the fine parts, the tower, the ball garage, the arm and two sets of optional legs.](/images/3d-prints-dispenser-slicer-v1.jpg)

The project fills six plates: the tower, the ball garage, the arm, the fine parts and two optional sets of legs. It takes almost a whole roll of filament and roughly 9 hours to print.

![The spiral ball garage of the dispenser printing in white on a Bambu Lab A1 mini](/media/3d-prints-dispenser-printing-v1.mp4 "/images/3d-prints-dispenser-printing-poster-v1.jpg")

![The finished dispenser tower in white, still on the print bed of the A1 mini](/images/3d-prints-dispenser-tower-v1.jpg)

Three things to know before printing:

- Use real golf balls. Foam balls are too light to work in it.
- The arm is the longest part. On a small printer like the A1 mini it prints in two pieces that must be glued together.
- The model is free to download under MakerWorld's Standard Digital File License, so technically it is not open source.

![The finished dispenser at work. A press of the green pedal swings the arm down and places a golf ball on the tee.](/media/3d-prints-dispenser-demo-v1.mp4 "/images/3d-prints-dispenser-demo-poster-v1.jpg")

## Golf Zwing Trainer

[Golf Zwing Trainer V4](https://www.printables.com/model/1163073-golf-zwing-trainer-v4) by WeighingMyOptions is a simple and effective tool for grooving swing plane. It is based on the Blue Brick training aid, so any training video made for it works for this one too. The design is in the public domain.

![The top of a green Zwing Trainer. Holes on each side are labeled 72 degrees for a sand wedge, 60 for a 6 iron and 48 for a driver, for left and right handers.](/images/3d-prints-zwing-top-v1.jpg)

Most beginners swing too steep. The trainer holds alignment sticks at set angles for a wedge, an iron and a driver, left or right handed, and swinging under the stick helps you feel a flatter swing plane.

![The Zwing Trainer on the floor holding two alignment sticks, one angled up to mark the swing plane and one flat along the target line](/images/3d-prints-zwing-in-use-v1.jpg)

A set of alignment sticks is needed. The holes are 9 mm wide, and I had to cut the rubber ends off my sticks for them to fit.

The base and lid close with four M5 screws, and the cavity inside needs weight so the trainer stays put. The documentation suggests weighing it down with pennies. I used what I had on hand: clay in one and BBs in another.

![The base of a green Zwing Trainer with its three cavities packed with clay, next to its lid](/images/3d-prints-zwing-clay-v1.jpg)

![The base of a blue Zwing Trainer with its three cavities filled with copper BBs](/images/3d-prints-zwing-bbs-v1.jpg)

![The lid of a green Zwing Trainer printing on a Bambu Lab A1 mini](/media/3d-prints-zwing-printing-v1.mp4 "/images/3d-prints-zwing-printing-poster-v1.jpg")

I recommend printing two. Used together, they give you a guide above and below your swing.

- [Golf Ball Dispenser Pro (MakerWorld)](https://makerworld.com/en/models/1295289-golf-ball-dispenser-pro)
- [Golf Zwing Trainer V4 (Printables)](https://www.printables.com/model/1163073-golf-zwing-trainer-v4)

title: OSSTagLab: Decoding the Sound of Golf Club Tags
body:
My curiosity around club tags started when someone borrowing my putter said, "Your putter is making weird noises." I couldn't hear a thing. It turns out the sound coming out of my putter was near ultrasonic.

My putter had an Arccos Gen 4 club tag screwed onto the end of the grip. I had been using club tags for around six months and I loved them. I recorded my lowest round with them and my longest drive. I learned about my miss tendencies and club distances on the course.

Overall, the software experience was smooth. However, when I wanted to play one of my favorite short par 3 courses, the 4 hole Joe Balander course in Austin, Texas, I ran into one of its shortcomings. The app reported 6 holes instead of the actual 4.

I emailed Arccos support and they told me the software simply didn't support 4 hole courses. They only supported 6, 9, 12, and 18 hole courses. This limitation seemed like a hard coded, arbitrary rule. Now I had motivation to go along with my curiosity. And so began the journey of [OSSTagLab](https://github.com/OSSGolf/osstaglab).

A shot tracking tag has one job: tell a phone which club left the bag and when it struck the ball. It does that with sound, in short tones between 17 and 20 [kHz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hertz), just above what most adults hear and well inside what a laptop microphone records.

A set of Arccos Gen 4 tags, a MacBook microphone and a flashlight were enough to work out what the tags are sending. OSSTagLab is the open source web app that came out of it, built to open club tagging to anybody.

![Spectrogram of a 9 iron tag over four seconds. A wake tone at 18.80 kHz, then the resting frame repeating around a rest tone of 17.91 kHz, then a hit and a hop pattern at 18.91 kHz.](/images/osstaglab-9-iron-timeline-v1.png)

## Listening at 18 kHz

A browser records the microphone at 48 kHz, which captures everything up to 24 kHz, the [Nyquist frequency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyquist_frequency). A [spectrogram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrogram) makes the result visible: time runs across, frequency runs up, brightness shows loudness. Under the hood it is a [short-time Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short-time_Fourier_transform): short slices of the recording, each shaped by a [Hann window](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hann_function) and passed through a [fast Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast_Fourier_transform).

The decoder takes a 10 ms slice every millisecond and keeps the strongest frequency between 16.5 and 21 kHz. What is left is a single line of frequency over time. A tag sends its data as steps up and down in that line, which is a form of [frequency-shift keying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frequency-shift_keying).

![The live spectrogram in OSSTagLab as four tags wake in turn. Each short dash is a wake tone and each comb below it is a resting frame repeating.](/images/osstaglab-live-wake-v1.png)

## Three Signals

A tag sends one tone at a time and rests near 18 kHz. Light wakes it up and a hit changes what it sends. That makes three signals to learn: a wake tone, a resting frame and an after hit signal.

## The Wake Tone

A tag wakes when light reaches it, as it does when a club leaves the bag. When it wakes up, it plays one steady tone for about 0.4 seconds, about 0.9 kHz above its rest tone. From driver to wedge, the clubs land between 18.68 and 18.92 kHz.

## The Resting Frame

Half a second later the tag settles onto its rest tone, between 17.78 and 18.02 kHz on this set. Every 172 ms it sends a frame of six symbols, each a 10 ms tone 1 to 4 steps of 100 Hz above or below the rest tone.

![Close view of one 9 iron resting frame. Six short tones step away from the 17.91 kHz rest tone by plus 4, minus 1, minus 2, plus 1, minus 4 and minus 3 steps of 100 Hz. The next frame starts 172 ms later.](/images/osstaglab-resting-frame-v1.png)

This 9 iron reads +4 −1 −2 +1 −4 −3. Each club has its own frame, so you only need to hear one frame to know which club it is.

## The After Hit Signal

The tag reacts to a hit within about 12 ms. The rest tone moves up 1 kHz and the tag begins to hop: up for about 21 ms, back down, and again at a fixed interval for several seconds, until the resting frame returns.

![The live spectrogram during a hit. The resting frame runs near 18 kHz, the tone moves up 1 kHz for the hop pattern, and the resting frame returns.](/images/osstaglab-live-hit-v1.png)

The size and pace of the hop change from club to club: 200, 300, 400 or 500 Hz, every 60, 80, 100 or 120 ms.

![Two spectrograms of the half second after a hit. The 9 iron jumps up 409 Hz every 61 ms. The 56 degree wedge jumps up 302 Hz every 122 ms.](/images/osstaglab-hop-patterns-v1.png)

The hop pattern tells you the club was hit. The resting frame right before it tells you which club it was.

## The Putter is Different

The putter is different from the moment it wakes up. Its wake tone is at 19.81 kHz, about 1 kHz above every other club in the bag.

![The OSSTagLab analysis view of a putter waking. A wake tone near 19.8 kHz, then the resting frame near 18 kHz.](/images/osstaglab-putter-wake-v1.png)

It also reacts to a hit differently. It stays on its rest tone and switches to a second frame for about two seconds. At rest it sends −4 −2 −1 −3 −1 +1, and after a hit it sends +1 +3 +4 +2 +4 −1.

![The OSSTagLab analysis view of a putter with each signal labeled. A wake tone at 19.8 kHz, the resting frame, a tap shown as a vertical line, the frame after the hit, then the resting frame again.](/images/osstaglab-putter-labeled-v1.png)

The vertical line is the tap, a short click across every frequency. The decoder listens for it between 2 and 8 kHz to work out when the hit happened.

## OSSTagLab

OSSTagLab puts all of this on one page. It runs on your own computer, listens through the browser, maps each club, names the club in hand and counts hits.

![Screenshot of the OSSTagLab web app. Club chips across the top, the spectrogram panel, a hits panel, and a saved clubs table with each club's resting frame, rest tone, wake tone and hop pattern.](/images/osstaglab-app-v1.png)

It needs Python 3.9 or newer and a browser.

```
git clone https://github.com/OSSGolf/osstaglab
cd osstaglab
python3 server.py
```

Open http://127.0.0.1:8765 and press **Start listening**. I recommend shining a flashlight at the club tags, since indoor light can be too dim to wake them.

The project is independent, built by listening to one set of tags. The decoder, its tests and short recordings are in the repo, so you can port it to a phone or a microcontroller.

The data from my club tags is in the repo, but yours will most likely be different. A frame holds six symbols with 8 possible values each, so there can be up to 262,144 unique club tag sounds.

- [osstaglab (web app, decoder, recordings)](https://github.com/OSSGolf/osstaglab)

title: Open Source Golf is Exploding
body:
People are building launch monitors, shot trackers, course databases, and simulator engines in the open, and the list keeps getting longer.

Here are the projects we are watching right now.

[![Open Source Golf Landscape: a map of 52 open source golf projects. Hardware covers launch monitors, on-course trackers, training aids, biomechanics and 3D printable gear. Software covers simulators, launch monitor connectivity, swing analysis, stats and scoring, course data and camera ball tracking.](/images/open-source-golf-landscape-map-v3-1920.png)](/images/open-source-golf-landscape-map-v3.png)

Tap the map to open it full size.

## Hardware

### Launch Monitors

#### Radar Based

- **[OpenFlight](https://github.com/open-flight/openflight)**: A DIY golf launch monitor built around the OPS243-A Doppler radar on a Raspberry Pi, reporting ball speed, club speed, smash factor and estimated carry, with an optional TI IWR6843 radar for launch angle.
  - **[openflight-enclosure](https://github.com/open-flight/openflight-enclosure)**: 3D-printable enclosure for an OpenFlight monitor, with separate STL parts for the shell, radar and camera fronts, screen bezel and feet, plus CAD source. Minimum print bed is 220 by 190 mm.
  - **[openflight-mobile-kmp](https://github.com/open-flight/openflight-mobile-kmp)**: A companion app for the OpenFlight launch monitor on Android and iOS, built with Kotlin Multiplatform and native UIs. It shows live shots, sessions and club stats over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth LE.
  - **[openflight-mobile](https://github.com/open-flight/openflight-mobile)**: An Expo (React Native) companion app for OpenFlight that connects to the server over a socket connection and mirrors the live shot data from the web UI.

#### Camera Based

- **[PiTrac](https://github.com/PiTracLM/PiTrac)**: A launch monitor that uses low-cost Raspberry Pi computers and cameras to measure ball launch speed, angles and spin in three dimensions. It feeds GSPro and E6/TruGolf simulators and a standalone web app.
- **[LaunchTrac](https://github.com/r87-e/LaunchTrac)**: A DIY golf launch monitor in Rust for a Raspberry Pi 5, using two global shutter cameras and IR strobes to measure ball speed, launch angles and spin.

#### Hybrid

- **[launch-monitor](https://github.com/thomasjhook/launch-monitor)**: A DIY golf launch monitor on a Raspberry Pi 5 that combines a camera for launch angle and spin, a 10.5 GHz Doppler radar with FFT for ball speed, and an IR trigger for timing.

### On-Course Trackers

#### GPS

- **[open-gps](https://github.com/open-flight/open-gps)**: A handheld golf shot tracker on an ESP32-S3 with a u-blox GPS module. It saves each shot's start and landing coordinates and distance in yards, exportable over USB as GeoJSON or CSV.

### Training Aids

#### Tempo

- **[OSSTempo](https://github.com/OSSGolf/osstempo)**: A golf tempo trainer built from an ESP32 and a WS2812B LED strip, where a light comet sweeps the strip to pace the stroke. A Web Bluetooth page controls it.
  - **[osstempo-ios](https://github.com/OSSGolf/osstempo-ios)**: A native SwiftUI and CoreBluetooth iPhone app that connects to the OSSTempo ESP32 trainer over Bluetooth LE, selects modes, triggers strokes and tunes settings with a live preview.

### Biomechanics

#### Force Plates

- **[open-fp](https://github.com/open-flight/open-fp)**: Open source golf force plates, one per foot, each with four 50 kg load cells read by an Arduino UNO Q. It reports vertical force, center of pressure and weight shift on a web dashboard. Still in hardware bring-up.

### 3D Printable

#### Swing Trainers

- **[Golf Zwing Trainer V4](https://www.printables.com/model/1163073-golf-zwing-trainer-v4)**: A 3D printable swing plane trainer for left and right handers. It holds printed alignment sticks at set angles to guide a shallower downswing, and the base can be weighted with lead or BBs.

#### Range Accessories

- **[Golf Ball Dispenser Pro](https://makerworld.com/en/models/1295289-golf-ball-dispenser-pro)**: A fully 3D printed golf ball dispenser with no extra hardware. Its magazine holds 25 balls and a foot pedal places one ball on the tee per press. Sized to print on an A1 mini.

## Software

### Simulators

#### Engines

- **[OpenShotGolf](https://github.com/jhauck2/OpenShotGolf)**: A Godot-based golf simulator that takes shot data from the PiTrac launch monitor or GSPro-style interfaces and models ball flight with drag and Magnus lift.
- **[Seneca-Golf](https://github.com/csites/Seneca-Golf)**: An open source golf simulator built on the Urho3D game engine, intended as a base for DIY launch monitor, course building and game design work.
- **[GolfForge](https://github.com/GolfForge/golfforge)**: An open source golf simulator built in Unreal Engine 5 that builds courses from LIDAR and OpenStreetMap data and accepts launch monitor input through GSPro Open Connect connectors.
- **[FUSE](https://github.com/OpenGolfSim/fuse)**: A lightweight 3D golf physics and simulation engine from OpenGolfSim for WebGL-capable browsers, built on Three.js and WebGPU. It is licensed under PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0.
- **[cyberflight](https://github.com/divotmaker/cyberflight)**: A Rust 3D driving range that displays shots received from flighthook, an open source golf automation bus, over a local WebSocket.
- **[Open-Birdie](https://github.com/rroojrooj/Open-Birdie)**: An Electron desktop golf simulator that plays OpenStreetMap courses with AWS terrain elevation data and accepts shots from GSPro Open Connect launch monitors such as the Uneekor EYEMINI LITE.
- **[uopengolf](https://github.com/digitalhand/uopengolf)**: An open source golf game for Windows and Linux built in Unreal Engine 5 with C++, with a savanna driving range, a 400-yard par 4, and Square Home or Open Connect launch monitor support.

#### Ball Flight Physics

- **[Simple-Golf-Simulator](https://github.com/markccchiang/Simple-Golf-Simulator)**: A Python and Tkinter program that simulates a golf swing from a two-degree-of-freedom model, then computes launch speed and the ball's flight with drag, lift, spin and wind.
- **[openfairway](https://github.com/digitalhand/openfairway)**: A Godot 4 physics addon, usable from C# and GDScript, that computes ball flight, bounce and surface interaction from aerodynamic drag and Magnus lift fits.
- **[libgolf](https://github.com/gdifiore/libgolf)**: A C++20 library that simulates a golf ball's full flight from launch conditions: aerial arc, bounce, and roll. Aerodynamics, bounce, and roll models are pluggable, and it builds to WebAssembly.
- **[dimple](https://github.com/divotmaker/dimple)**: A pure Rust crate, with no dependencies, that turns launch-monitor numbers into a full golf shot: flight, bounce, and roll on turf. Air density and wind are configurable.

#### Course Building

- **[TGC-Designer-Tools](https://github.com/chadrockey/TGC-Designer-Tools)**: Python tools for course creation and lidar terrain generation in The Golf Club 2019. The main entry points are a GUI, a lidar map API, and an image-based terrain tool.
- **[course-terrain-tool](https://github.com/OpenGolfSim/course-terrain-tool)**: A desktop app that searches free lidar sources, merges and crops LAZ or DEM files, and outputs raw Unity height maps and satellite overlay images for golf simulator courses.
- **[course-meshery-tool](https://github.com/OpenGolfSim/course-meshery-tool)**: A JavaScript course-building tool from OpenGolfSim that generates base course meshes from an SVG file and a raw height map.

### Launch Monitor Connectivity

#### Protocol Libraries

- **[gsp-r10-adapter](https://github.com/mholow/gsp-r10-adapter)**: A C# utility that bridges a Garmin Approach R10 launch monitor to GSPro, with direct Bluetooth, an E6 Connect compatible server, and webcam putting options.
- **[10over](https://github.com/divotmaker/10over)**: A Rust client library for the Garmin R10 Bluetooth protocol that decodes BLE, GFDI, and protobuf messages into shot data through a poll-based API.
- **[ironsight](https://github.com/divotmaker/ironsight)**: A Rust client library for the FlightScope Mevo+, Mevo Gen2, and Xi radar launch monitors, speaking their binary protocol over TCP with a poll-based API.
- **[allsquare](https://github.com/divotmaker/allsquare)**: A Rust client library for the Square Golf Omni launch monitor's BLE protocol, reporting ball and club metrics through a poll-based API, plus a Flight Relay launch monitor binary.
- **[R10Kit](https://github.com/OSSGolf/unofficial-r10-ios-sdk)**: A pure Swift package that connects to a Garmin R10 launch monitor over Bluetooth Low Energy and exposes shot metrics, including practice swings without a ball, for iOS, watchOS and macOS apps.
- **[Flight Relay Protocol](https://github.com/flightrelay/spec)**: An open JSON message spec, released under CC0, for sending launch monitor shot data over a local WebSocket to simulators, stat trackers and other tools.

#### Bridges to Simulators

- **[MLM2PRO-GSPro-Connector](https://github.com/springbok/MLM2PRO-GSPro-Connector)**: A Windows GUI application written in Python that sends Rapsodo MLM2PRO and Mevo+ shots to GSPro, with optional webcam or ExPutt putting support.
- **[MLM2PRO-BT-APP](https://github.com/Duwaynef/MLM2PRO-BT-APP)**: A beta Windows app in C# that connects a Rapsodo MLM2PRO to simulator software over direct Bluetooth through the Open API, with an optional API relay for other connectors.
- **[GSPro-MLM2PRO-OCR](https://github.com/rowengb/GSPro-MLM2PRO-OCR-Connector)**: A Python app that reads Rapsodo MLM2PRO metrics from a mirrored phone or tablet screen using OpenCV and Tesseract OCR, then sends them to GSPro.
- **[flighthook](https://github.com/divotmaker/flighthook)**: A Rust bridge that decodes shots from launch monitors such as FlightScope, Square Golf Omni and Garmin R10, and forwards them to simulators like GSPro.
- **[gspro-bridge](https://github.com/brettveenstra/gspro-bridge)**: A C# Windows bridge, in early development, intended to send Garmin R10 and optional webcam putting shots to GSPro. The README says it is not yet ready for use.
- **[fairway-bridge](https://github.com/401Unauthorized/fairway-bridge)**: A Go application that connects launch monitors, simulators and cameras over a network, with a web UI, shot data logging to CSV, and virtual shot emulation for testing.

### Swing Analysis

#### Video and Pose

- **[GolfPosePro](https://github.com/ryanboscobanze/GolfPosePro)**: A Jupyter notebook for Google Colab that uses MediaPipe Pose to track wrist motion, split a swing into phases, and compare student and pro frames in annotated slow-motion videos.
- **[GolfSwingAnalyzer](https://github.com/ktakenos/GolfSwingAnalyzer)**: A Python PyQt5 app that estimates body joints in 3D from two synchronized videos of a swing, plotting the skeleton with OpenGL and exporting joint coordinates to CSV.
- **[Pose2Par](https://github.com/cavanaulton/Pose2Par)**: A desktop UI and Docker pipeline that turns a standard swing video into biomechanical data using MMPose pose estimation, ML marker enhancement and OpenSim. It reports pelvis and torso rotation, X-factor and swing event timing.
- **[golf-swing-analysis](https://github.com/HeleenaRobert/golf-swing-analysis)**: A Python script that tracks ear, hip and wrist landmarks with MediaPipe Pose on a down-the-line swing video, draws the swing angle and an X/Y axis overlay, and saves an annotated MP4.
- **[PinPoint Studio](https://github.com/PinPoint-Golf/PinPointStudio)**: A beta, cross-platform desktop app in C++ and Qt for swing analysis. It combines multi-camera video, IMU wrist sensors and launch monitors, runs pose estimation locally, and reports metrics for each shot.
  - **[PinPointCapture](https://github.com/PinPoint-Golf/PinPointCapture)**: The iPhone companion app for PinPoint Studio, which joins a session as a camera over WiFi or USB. This repository also holds its requirements, design mockups and protocol conformance records.

#### Wearable

- **[iSwing](https://github.com/ChillVeen/iSwing)**: A watchOS and iOS app that records golf swings with Apple Watch motion sensors and reports swing speed, attack angle, tempo and a machine-learning quality rating.

### Camera Ball Tracking

#### Putting

- **[cam-putting-py](https://github.com/alleexx/cam-putting-py)**: A webcam putting simulator for GSPro that tracks a colored ball to calculate putt speed in mph and horizontal launch angle. Shots go to a Garmin R10 or MLM2PRO connector, which passes them to GSPro.

### Course Data

#### Databases and APIs

- **[golf-data-docs](https://github.com/Jacobbrewer1/golf-data-docs)**: Generated documentation for the Golf Data API, covering clubs, courses, markers and holes. The API currently holds only UK course data.
- **[OpenGolfAPI](https://github.com/opengolfapi/api)**: A community-maintained REST API for golf courses worldwide, with tee sets, hole-by-hole data, climate normals and nearby places. No key is needed for 1,000 requests a day per IP; a free key raises the limit.
  - **[mcp-server](https://github.com/opengolfapi/mcp-server)**: An MCP server that lets AI assistants search golf courses, scorecards, tees and weather from OpenGolfAPI, with an optional free key for logging shots and running tournaments.
- **[GeoJSON-GolfCourses](https://github.com/TheMapSmith/GeoJSON-GolfCourses)**: A GeoJSON file of named golf course boundaries in North America, extracted from OpenStreetMap ways tagged leisure=golf_course. European courses are listed as coming soon.

### Stats and Scoring

#### Launch Monitor Data

- **[TrackPull](https://github.com/criticalberne/TrackPull)**: A Chrome extension that pulls shot data from Trackman reports and Trackman portal sessions, then exports it as CSV, copies it to Google Sheets, or builds a prompt for an AI chatbot.
- **[r10progress](https://github.com/thraizz/r10progress)**: A TypeScript web app that imports CSV shot exports from the Garmin Approach R10 radar, stores them in Firebase, and charts shot trends with Vega and a sortable ag-Grid table.

#### Rounds and Handicap

- **[garmin_golf](https://github.com/gsingers/garmin_golf)**: Browser scripts that export your own Garmin Connect golf scorecards and CT10 shot data as JSON, since Garmin has no public API. Includes jq and Google Sheets processing.
- **[ghin](https://github.com/n8io/ghin)**: An unofficial TypeScript library, installed from npm, that wraps the GHIN handicap API for handicap lookups, golfer and course search, scoring history and course handicap calculation.
- **[golf-app](https://github.com/gmalewicz/golf-app)**: A Java Spring Boot back-end for online scorecards, round results including Stableford and score differential, tournaments, and player result comparison.
- **[opengolfapp](https://github.com/cner-smith/opengolfapp)**: A free, open source golf tracking app for web, iOS and Android, with a React web app and Expo mobile app that logs shots, computes strokes gained, shot dispersion and handicap index.

#### Tour Data

- **[data-golf-api](https://github.com/coreyjs/data-golf-api)**: An unofficial Python client for the DataGolf API, installed from PyPI as data_golf, covering general, prediction, betting and historical endpoints. Requires a paid DataGolf API key.

We will keep adding to this list as more projects show up.

Software covers simulators, launch monitor connectivity, swing analysis, stats and scoring, course data and camera ball tracking.

title: Introducing OSSGolf
body:
Have you ever seen an overpriced golf gadget and thought "I could build that"?

You probably could. That is the whole idea behind OSSGolf.

Golf has a proud DIY history. Long before the big brands, players forged their own irons, turned persimmon heads by hand, and tweaked shafts in the garage until something worked. Tinkering helped build this game. Somewhere along the way, we handed all of it over to a checkout page.

Other hobbies never let that spirit die. People design and build experimental aircraft in their garages and actually fly them. Ham radio operators still solder their own rigs. There is no reason golf training should be any different.

OSSGolf brings it back. Open, free hardware and software for real training aids, documented well enough that you can build them yourself. A tempo trainer that costs tens of dollars in parts instead of the hundred plus you would pay off the shelf. A launch monitor SDK that lets your phone read a device you already own, with no subscription and no extra hardware.

The point is that you build it, you own it, you understand it, and you can change it.

Good training should not be locked behind a premium price tag. If you have ever wanted to build your own, this is the place.

Everything is open on GitHub: [github.com/OSSGolf](https://github.com/OSSGolf).

title: OSSTempo: A DIY LED Tempo Trainer for Golf
body:
OSSTempo is an open source golf tempo trainer. A WS2812B LED strip animates a moving "comet" of light that sweeps along a channel, and you match your putter or club head to the dot to groove a consistent stroke.

It is a TempoStik style trainer built entirely from open hardware and firmware. An ESP32 drives a 144 LED per meter strip over a single data pin. You control it over Bluetooth Low Energy, so a web page or the companion iOS app can set the tempo and stroke length.

Here it is running a putting stroke:

![OSSTempo running a putting stroke on a practice mat: the white comet sweeps the LED strip beside the ball while the green dot marks impact, powered by an ESP32 on a breadboard](/media/osstempo-putting.mp4 "/images/osstempo-still.jpg")

## Two Modes

- **Putting (2:1).** The comet sweeps from center out to the top of the backswing, eases to a stop, then accelerates back through center at impact and out the far side on the follow through.
- **Full swing.** The firmware models a full swing arc projected onto the one dimensional strip, so a one meter strip can represent a stroke that travels back and up behind you. Reference dots mark the ball, the top of the backswing, and an optional aim point.

## Build It Two Ways

Same firmware, same app, two hardware paths:

- **Full DIY.** A bare ESP32 dev board, a strip, one resistor, and one capacitor on a breadboard. This is the cheapest option.
- **QuinLED Dig2go.** A pre assembled controller.

Both are documented end to end: bill of materials, wiring, flashing, and a pinned, ready to flash sketch.

## Print a Case and a Jig

The repo now has two 3D printed parts. Each comes with STL files and a Bambu Studio project for the A1 mini.

**Case.** A snap shut case for the carrier PCB, an optional board the ESP32 plugs into. The board sits on four pegs through its mounting holes and the lid clips on by hand, with openings for the USB and strip cables. The golf ball badge and the oss/golf nameplate are separate parts that press into the lid, so they can be printed in a second color.

![Render of the 3D printed OSSTempo case, closed: an orange lid with a golf ball badge and an oss/golf nameplate set into it in a second color](/images/osstempo-case-closed.jpg)

![Render of the case open: the carrier board sits on four pegs in the base, with the lid, the golf ball badge and the nameplate beside it](/images/osstempo-case-open.jpg)

**Alignment jig.** A flat plate that holds two sticks parallel, 8 inches apart, with alignment lines grooved along it.

![Render of the 3D printed alignment jig: a flat plate with a channel at each end for a stick and alignment lines grooved along it](/images/osstempo-alignment-jig.jpg)

## What is Here Today

The firmware, the Web Bluetooth control page, and a native SwiftUI iOS controller are all open source and working on real hardware. The build guides cover both hardware paths.

The clip above shows a putting stroke on a practice mat. For the full hardware spec and code, see GitHub.

- [osstempo (firmware, web control, docs)](https://github.com/OSSGolf/osstempo)
- [osstempo-ios (native iOS controller)](https://github.com/OSSGolf/osstempo-ios)

title: R10Kit: An Unofficial Swift SDK for the Garmin R10
body:
R10Kit is a native Swift SDK that connects directly to the Garmin Approach R10 launch monitor over Bluetooth Low Energy. No first party app, no PC tether. Your iPhone talks to the R10 and reads every shot it sends.

> This is an unofficial SDK. The protocol layer is reverse engineered from publicly available work ([mholow/gsp-r10-adapter](https://github.com/mholow/gsp-r10-adapter)).

## The Practice Swing Unlock

The interesting part is what the R10 gives you without a ball. On a full practice swing with no ball, the radar still reports club speed, club path, attack angle, and the full swing timing in milliseconds. R10Kit exposes all of it. That means you can build a tempo trainer around a launch monitor you already own, not just a ball flight tracer.

Ball metrics (ball speed, launch angle and direction, spin rate, spin axis) are filled in only when the radar sees a ball leave. Everything else is filled in on every swing.

## Screenshots

The repo ships a runnable demo app. It shows connection state, device info, and a live list of recent shots. Tap a shot to see every field the SDK exposes.

![R10Kit demo showing connection state, device model and firmware, battery level, and a list of recent shots labeled by club speed](/images/r10-shot-list.png)

![Shot detail showing identity fields and club metrics: club speed, club path, and attack angle](/images/r10-shot-detail.png)

![Shot detail scrolled to swing timing and the derived metrics: backswing, downswing, follow through, total duration, and tempo ratio](/images/r10-tempo.png)

## What It Parses

R10Kit does full proto parsing for every shot the device sends: club speed, ball speed, launch angle and direction, spin rate with axis and provenance, attack angle, club face and path, swing timing in milliseconds, shot type, and tilt at impact. The API is AsyncStream first, modern Swift Concurrency, no delegates.

- iOS 17+, watchOS 10+, macOS 14+. Pure Swift package.
- 70 unit tests covering framing, COBS, CRC, proto parsing, time base conversion, and the swing rejection detector.
- Real byte regression fixtures captured from the device, so future changes cannot silently break protocol compatibility.

Tested against an R10 on firmware 4.50 with an iPhone 16 Pro.

## Get It

- [unofficial-r10-ios-sdk on GitHub](https://github.com/OSSGolf/unofficial-r10-ios-sdk)

Builds on [mholow/gsp-r10-adapter](https://github.com/mholow/gsp-r10-adapter), under the same MIT license.
